content: Protecting accounts with Time-Based One-Time Passwords (TOTP). A visual and technical guide to implementing 2FA, generating QR codes, and handling recovery flows in Go.
title: Double the Security: Implementing Two-Factor Authentication (TOTP)

content: IntroductionPasswords are distinctively terrible. Users reuse them. Users choose “Password123”. Users write them on sticky notes. Even with strong password policies, a database leak from another site can compromise your users. Two-Factor Authentication (2FA) mitigates this by requiring a second factor: something physically in the user’s possession (their phone). In this guide, we implement standard TOTP (Time-based One-Time Password), compatible with Google Authenticator, Authy, and Microsoft Authenticator.
title: Double the Security: Implementing Two-Factor Authentication (TOTP)

content: 1. Understanding TOTP (RFC 6238)TOTP is built on top of HOTP (HMAC-based One-Time Password).
title: Double the Security: Implementing Two-Factor Authentication (TOTP)

content: The Algorithm$$TOTP(K, T) = Truncate(HMAC-SHA-1(K, T))$$ Where: $K$ is the Shared Secret (a random string of bytes known only to Server and User). $T$ is the Time Counter, calculated as $\lfloor \frac{CurrentUnixTime}{30} \rfloor$. 30 is the standard step size (seconds). Every 30 seconds, the value $T$ increments by 1. The algorithms on the phone and server independently run the HMAC hash and produce the same 6-digit code.
title: Double the Security: Implementing Two-Factor Authentication (TOTP)

content: 2. Implementation Lifecycle
title: Double the Security: Implementing Two-Factor Authentication (TOTP)

content: 2.1 Setup (Enable 2FA)When a user wants to enable 2FA: Generate Secret: We generate a cryptographically secure random key (20 bytes). Generate URI: We format this into a standard URL scheme: otpauth://totp/Golang4U:user@email.com?secret=JBSWY3DPEHPK3PXP&issuer=Golang4U Generate QR Code: We render this URL as a QR code image (PNG) so the user can scan it. Go Code (using pquerna/otp): import ( "github.com/pquerna/otp/totp" "bytes" "image/png" ) func Generate2FASetup(email string) (*totp.Key, []byte, error) { // Generate Key key, err := totp.Generate(totp.GenerateOpts{ Issuer: "Golang4U", AccountName: email, }) if err != nil { return nil, nil, err } // Generate QR Code Image var buf bytes.Buffer img, err := key.Image(200, 200) png.Encode(&buf, img) return key, buf.Bytes(), nil }
title: Double the Security: Implementing Two-Factor Authentication (TOTP)

content: 2.2 Verification (The Handshake)We cannot enable 2FA just because we generated a key. The user must prove they scanned it successfully. Frontend displays QR Code. User scans it and enters the 6-digit code (123456) shown on their screen. Server validates 123456 against the generated secret. Only if valid, we save the Secret to the User’s DB profile (Encrypted!) and set two_factor_enabled = true.
title: Double the Security: Implementing Two-Factor Authentication (TOTP)

content: 2.3 Login Flow with 2FAOnce enabled, the login flow changes: sequenceDiagramparticipant Userparticipant ServerUser->>Server: POST /login (email, password)Server->>Server: Verify Passwordalt 2FA EnabledServer-->>User: 200 OK { status: "2fa_required", temp_token: "..." }User->>Server: POST /verify-2fa (code: "123456", temp_token)Server->>Server: totp.Validate(code, userSecret)Server-->>User: 200 OK { token: "PASETO..." }else No 2FAServer-->>User: 200 OK { token: "PASETO..." }endThe “Temp Token”: This is a critical security detail. The initial response must not be a valid session token. It should be a restricted token that only allows access to the /verify-2fa endpoint. In Golang4U, we use a PASETO with a special scope: "pre-auth".
title: Double the Security: Implementing Two-Factor Authentication (TOTP)

content: 3. Recovery: The “Bus Factor”What if the user drops their phone in a lake? They are locked out forever. This is why Recovery Codes are mandatory. When 2FA is enabled, we generate 5-10 random strings (e.g., a1b2-c3d4). User Side: “Save these codes in a safe place.” Server Side: We Hash them (bcrypt) and store them in a recovery_codes collection. If the user cannot generate a TOTP, they can use a Recovery Code. Server verifies Code against Hash. Important: The used code is immediately deleted from the DB. Use only once.
title: Double the Security: Implementing Two-Factor Authentication (TOTP)

content: 4. Security Considerations Time Drift: Clocks aren’t perfect. We allow a verification window of 1 step (current time +/- 30 seconds) to account for slight network or device delays. Rate Limiting: The /verify-2fa endpoint MUST be strictly rate-limited (e.g., 3 attempts per minute). 6 digits is only 1 million combinations; a brute force attack is trivial without rate limiting. Encrypted Secrets: The TOTP secret in the database allows anyone with read access to clone the user’s 2FA device. This field MUST be encrypted with AES-GCM (as discussed in the Cryptography article).
title: Double the Security: Implementing Two-Factor Authentication (TOTP)

content: ConclusionBy implementing TOTP, Golang4U aligns with industry best practices for account security. It adds a trivial amount of friction for a massive gain in trust. Combined with our ECIES encryption and PASETO tokens, our authentication system is defense-in-depth incarnate. This concludes our deep dive series into the Golang4U architecture. We hope these articles have provided you with a clear roadmap for building your own secure, scalable Go applications.
title: Double the Security: Implementing Two-Factor Authentication (TOTP)

content: A masterclass in application-layer cryptography. Learn how Golang4U implements ECIES to encrypt data in the browser and AES-GCM to secure data at rest.
title: Encryption Everywhere: End-to-End Security with ECIES and AES-GCM

content: IntroductionHTTPS (TLS) is fantastic. It encrypts the pipe between the user and your server. But what happens if: You have a load balancer or CDN that terminates TLS before the request reaches your app? You have a compromised middleware logging requests? You want to ensure nobody, not even your infrastructure provider, can read a user’s password in transit? This is where Application-Layer Encryption comes in. In Golang4U, we use ECIES (Elliptic Curve Integrated Encryption Scheme) for data in transit (Frontend -> Backend) and AES-GCM for data at rest.
title: Encryption Everywhere: End-to-End Security with ECIES and AES-GCM

content: 1. Understanding ECIES (Conceptual)ECIES is a hybrid encryption scheme. It combines the best of Asymmetric (Public Key) and Symmetric (Shared Key) cryptography. The Actors: Alice (Browser): Wants to send a secret message. Bob (Server): Has a static Public Key ($Pub_B$). The Workflow: Key Generation: Alice generates a temporary (ephemeral) key pair ($Priv_A, Pub_A$). Key Agreement (ECDH): Alice uses her $Priv_A$ and Bob’s $Pub_B$ to mathematically derive a Shared Secret ($S$). Encryption: Alice encrypts the message with AES using $K_{enc}$ derived from $S$. Transmission: Alice sends her Public Key ($Pub_A$) along with the ciphertext. sequenceDiagramparticipant Browser (Alice)participant Hacker (Eve)participant Server (Bob)Note over Server (Bob): Has Static Keypair (PrivB, PubB)Browser (Alice)->>Server (Bob): GET /public-keyServer (Bob)-->>Browser (Alice): Sends PubBNote over Browser (Alice): 1. Generates Ephemeral (PrivA, PubA)Note over Browser (Alice): 2. Computes S = ECDH(PrivA, PubB)Note over Browser (Alice): 3. Encrypts Msg with AES(S)Browser (Alice)->>Server (Bob): POST [PubA] + [Ciphertext]Note right of Hacker (Eve): Sees PubA and Ciphertext.Note right of Hacker (Eve): Cannot compute S without PrivA or PrivB!Note over Server (Bob): 1. Receives PubANote over Server (Bob): 2. Computes S = ECDH(PrivB, PubA)Note over Server (Bob): 3. Decrypts Msg with AES(S)Bob receives it, does the math in reverse, regenerates $K_{enc}$, and decrypts the message.
title: Encryption Everywhere: End-to-End Security with ECIES and AES-GCM

content: 2. Frontend Implementation (Web Crypto API)We don’t need heavy JS libraries. Modern browsers support SubtleCrypto. // assets/js/crypto_utils.js (Simplified) async function encryptData(plaintext, serverPublicKeyHex) { // 1. Import Server's Public Key const serverKey = await window.crypto.subtle.importKey( "spki", hexToArrayBuffer(serverPublicKeyHex), { name: "ECDH", namedCurve: "P-256" }, false, [] ); // 2. Generate Ephemeral Key Pair for this encryption const ephemeralKeyPair = await window.crypto.subtle.generateKey( { name: "ECDH", namedCurve: "P-256" }, true, ["deriveKey"] ); // 3. Derive Shared Secret (AES-GCM key) const sharedKey = await window.crypto.subtle.deriveKey( { name: "ECDH", public: serverKey }, ephemeralKeyPair.privateKey, { name: "AES-GCM", length: 256 }, false, ["encrypt"] ); // 4. Encrypt const iv = window.crypto.getRandomValues(new Uint8Array(12)); const encrypted = await window.crypto.subtle.encrypt( { name: "AES-GCM", iv: iv }, sharedKey, new TextEncoder().encode(plaintext) ); // 5. Pack: EphemeralPublicKey + IV + Ciphertext return pack(ephemeralKeyPair.publicKey, iv, encrypted); } This effectively creates a secure tunnel inside the HTTPS tunnel.
title: Encryption Everywhere: End-to-End Security with ECIES and AES-GCM

content: 3. Backend Implementation (Go crypto/ecdh)On the Go side, we parse this package. // internal/crypto/ecies.go func Decrypt(payload []byte, serverPrivKey *ecdh.PrivateKey) ([]byte, error) { // 1. Unpack payload // [Pub Key (65 bytes)] [IV (12 bytes)] [Ciphertext (rest)] clientPubKeyBytes := payload[:65] iv := payload[65:77] ciphertext := payload[77:] // 2. Parse Client's Ephemeral Public Key clientPubKey, err := ecdh.P256().NewPublicKey(clientPubKeyBytes) if err != nil { return nil, err } // 3. ECDH: Derive Shared Secret sharedSecret, err := serverPrivKey.ECDH(clientPubKey) if err != nil { return nil, err } // 4. Derive AES Key (using HKDF or similar standard, usually just the secret directly if simple) // In strict ECIES, we use KDF. For simple P-256+AES-GCM, we might just use the secret if 32 bytes // or run it through SHA-256. block, _ := aes.NewCipher(sharedSecret) gcm, _ := cipher.NewGCM(block) // 5. Decrypt return gcm.Open(nil, iv, ciphertext, nil) }
title: Encryption Everywhere: End-to-End Security with ECIES and AES-GCM

content: Why P-256?We chose the NIST P-256 curve because: Hardware Support: It has hardware acceleration on most CPUs (AES-NI). Browser Standard: It is universally supported by the Web Crypto API.
title: Encryption Everywhere: End-to-End Security with ECIES and AES-GCM

content: 4. Securing Data at Rest: AES-GCMOnce we decrypt the data, we might need to store it. Passwords: NEVER encrypt passwords. Always Hash them (Argon2 / bcrypt). PII (Emails, Phones): Encrypt. Tokens (OAuth, 2FA): Encrypt. We use AES-GCM (Galois/Counter Mode).
title: Encryption Everywhere: End-to-End Security with ECIES and AES-GCM

content: Authenticated EncryptionAES in CBC (Cipher Block Chaining) mode is malleable. If an attacker flips a bit in the ciphertext, it decrypts to garbage—or worse, specific garbage. GCM solves this by adding an “Authentication Tag”. If the ciphertext is tampered with (even 1 bit), the decryption function returns an error authentication failed rather than corrupt data. func EncryptStorage(plaintext []byte) ([]byte, error) { // Master Key loaded from secure env block, _ := aes.NewCipher(masterKey) gcm, _ := cipher.NewGCM(block) // ALWAYS use a random Nonce nonce := make([]byte, gcm.NonceSize()) io.ReadFull(rand.Reader, nonce) // Seal = Encrypt + Append Auth Tag return gcm.Seal(nonce, nonce, plaintext, nil), nil }
title: Encryption Everywhere: End-to-End Security with ECIES and AES-GCM

content: The Nonce DangersThe Nonce (Number used ONCE) is critical. If you reuse a nonce with the same key, an attacker can XOR the ciphertexts to recover the plaintext. Fix: We randomly generate a 12-byte nonce for every encryption operation and store it alongside the ciphertext.
title: Encryption Everywhere: End-to-End Security with ECIES and AES-GCM

content: ConclusionCryptography is a double-edged sword. Implemented correctly, it provides mathematical certainty of privacy. Implemented poorly (reused nonces, weak curves), it provides a false sense of security. Golang4U adheres to strict standards: ECDH P-256 for key exchange, AES-256-GCM for encryption, and standard Web Crypto APIs. This ensures our user’s data remains theirs, regardless of who is listening on the wire. In the final post of our series, we tackle the implementation of Two-Factor Authentication (TOTP) to secure user accounts.
title: Encryption Everywhere: End-to-End Security with ECIES and AES-GCM

content: A comprehensive masterclass on the history and future of token-based authentication. We analyze the cryptographic failures of JWT, the security-by-design of PASETO, and the emerging standard for key management: PASERK.
title: The Evolution of Authentication: JWT, PASETO, and PASERK

content: IntroductionAuthentication is the bedrock of modern application security. For years, developers have reached for JWT (JSON Web Tokens) as the default tool for stateless authentication. But standards evolve. Vulnerabilities are found. Better tools are built. In this deep dive, we will trace the evolution of token security: Generation 1: JWT (RFC 7519) - The Standard with Footguns. Generation 2: PASETO (Platform-Agnostic Security Tokens) - The Secure Replacement. Generation 3: PASERK (Platform-Agnostic SERialized Keys) - The Key Management Layer. We will strictly analyze why Golang4U moved to PASETO and how it prepares us for a PASERK future.
title: The Evolution of Authentication: JWT, PASETO, and PASERK

content: Part 1: The JWT Era (and its Cracks)JWTs are flexible. Too flexible. A JWT header looks like this: { "alg": "HS256", "typ": "JWT" } The alg field tells the server how to verify the token. This design choice—letting the client specify the crypto—led to catastrophic vulnerabilities.
title: The Evolution of Authentication: JWT, PASETO, and PASERK

content: 1.1 The “None” AlgorithmThe spec defined alg: none for debugging. Attack: An attacker sends a token with {"alg": "none"} and removes the signature. Result: Naive libraries see “none”, skip verification, and accept the token as valid.
title: The Evolution of Authentication: JWT, PASETO, and PASERK

content: 1.2 Algorithm Confusion (The RSA -> HMAC Attack)This is a classic cryptographic downgrade attack. Scenario: Server supports RS256 (Public/Private key) but also HS256 (Shared secret). Attack: Attacker gets the Server’s Public Key (it’s public!). Attacker creates a malicious token. Attacker sets header to {"alg": "HS256"}. Attacker signs the token using the Public Key as the HMAC secret. Result: The server sees HS256, looks up its verification key (which it thinks is the Public Key), treats it as an HMAC secret, hashes the token, and… IT MATCHES. The attacker has forged a valid token using only public data.
title: The Evolution of Authentication: JWT, PASETO, and PASERK

content: Part 2: PASETO (The Fix)PASETO (Platform-Agnostic Security Tokens) was designed by security experts to eliminate these choices. It is versioned, not negotiated.
title: The Evolution of Authentication: JWT, PASETO, and PASERK

content: 2.1 The Formatv4.public.payload.footer v4: Defines the exact cipher suite. No choices. No implementation errors. public: Defines the purpose (Public Key Signatures).
title: The Evolution of Authentication: JWT, PASETO, and PASERK

content: 2.2 Why v4?Golang4U uses PASETO v4 because it uses state-of-the-art cryptography: Signatures: Ed25519. Fast, constant-time, and resistant to side-channel attacks. Encryption: XChaCha20-Poly1305. A stream cipher that is faster than AES on mobile devices and doesn’t require hardware acceleration to be secure.
title: The Evolution of Authentication: JWT, PASETO, and PASERK

content: 2.3 Implementation in GoIn Golang4U, we use aidantwoods/go-paseto. Here is how we enforce strict security rules. // internal/token/paseto_maker.go func (maker *PasetoMaker) VerifyToken(token string) (*PasetoPayload, error) { parser := paseto.NewParser() // Rule 1: Must not be expired parser.AddRule(paseto.NotExpired()) // Rule 2: Must be issued by US parser.AddRule(paseto.IssuedBy("Golang4U")) // Rule 3: Must be intended for 'access' (not refresh) parser.AddRule(paseto.Subject("access_token")) parsedToken, err := parser.ParseV4Public(maker.publicKey, token, nil) if err != nil { return nil, ErrInvalidToken } return payloadFromToken(parsedToken), nil }
title: The Evolution of Authentication: JWT, PASETO, and PASERK

content: Part 3: PASERK (The Future of Keys)So we have secure tokens. But how do we manage the Keys? If I send you a string d8291..., is it a Public Key? A Private Key? An AES key? Algorithm specific? This is where PASERK (Platform-Agnostic SERialized Keys) comes in. It is to Keys what PASETO is to Tokens.
title: The Evolution of Authentication: JWT, PASETO, and PASERK

content: 3.1 The Problem PASERK Solves“Key Confusion” is as dangerous as Token Algorithm confusion. If you accidentally paste a Private Key into a Public Key configuration field, you might expose your secrets.
title: The Evolution of Authentication: JWT, PASETO, and PASERK

content: 3.2 The FormatPASERK wraps keys in a type-safe, versioned string format. k4.public.d82... -> This is clearly a v4 Public Key. k4.secret.a19... -> This is clearly a v4 Secret Key. k4.lid... -> Local Key ID.
title: The Evolution of Authentication: JWT, PASETO, and PASERK

content: 3.3 Wrapping Keys (Key Wrapping)PASERK also defines standard ways to encrypt keys for transport. Example: k4.seal... This allows us to store our Ed25519 private keys in the database, encrypted by a Master Key, in a standard format that any PASERK-aware library can decrypt. Theoretical Implementation: // Future-proofing Golang4U with PASERK func RotateKeys() string { // Generate new Keypair secretKey := paseto.NewV4AsymmetricSecretKey() // Serialize to PASERK for safe storage paserkString := secretKey.ExportPaserk() // "k4.secret....." // In the future, we might wrap this with a master key // wrapped := paserk.Wrap(masterKey, secretKey) return paserkString }
title: The Evolution of Authentication: JWT, PASETO, and PASERK

content: Part 4: Beyond the Token (mTLS & Hitless TLS)Secure authentication is only one layer correctly. As we scale Golang4U, we look at the transport layer itself.
title: The Evolution of Authentication: JWT, PASETO, and PASERK

content: 4.1 mTLS (Mutual TLS)Standard TLS proves the Server’s identity to the Client (“You are really google.com”). mTLS proves the Client’s identity to the Server (“You are really valid-service-A”). In a microservices architecture (e.g., if we split Golang4U into AuthService and PostService), we would use mTLS. PostService presents a Client Certificate signed by our internal CA. AuthService verifies the certificate. If valid, the connection is allowed. This happens before any PASETO token is even sent. It is “Zero Trust” networking.
title: The Evolution of Authentication: JWT, PASETO, and PASERK

content: 4.2 Hitless TLS (Session Resumption)Establishing a TLS handshake is expensive (multiple round-trips). Hitless TLS (or Session Resumption) allows a client to reconnect quickly without a full handshake, using a Session Ticket. Danger: If the “Ticket Key” on the server is compromised, all previous sessions can be decrypted (Forward Secrecy violation). Golang4U Key Rotation: We configure our tls.Config to rotate Session Ticket Keys hourly, preserving Forward Secrecy while maintaining performance.
title: The Evolution of Authentication: JWT, PASETO, and PASERK

content: ConclusionSecurity is a moving target. JWT served us well but showed its age with cryptographic footguns. PASETO fixes the protocol level, giving us versioned, secure-by-default tokens. PASERK simplifies the management of the keys themselves. By choosing PASETO v4 (Ed25519) today, Golang4U is well-positioned to adopt PASERK and mTLS strategies as we scale from a monolith to a distributed system.
title: The Evolution of Authentication: JWT, PASETO, and PASERK

content: A deep technical guide on implementing defense-in-depth in Go. We create a custom IP Filtering middleware, implement granular Rate Limiting, and configure secure HTTP headers to prevent XSS and Clickjacking.
title: Fortifying the Backend: Advanced IP Filtering, Rate Limiting, and Headers

content: IntroductionIn the modern internet landscape, deploying a backend without protection is akin to leaving your front door wide open. Automated bots, script kiddies, and targeted attackers are constantly scanning for vulnerabilities. “Working code” is not enough. We need Secure Code. In this article, we will implement three layers of defense for our Go backend: Network Layer Defense: Application-level IP Filtering. Traffic Control: Granular Rate Limiting/Throttling. Browser Defense: Secure HTTP Headers.
title: Fortifying the Backend: Advanced IP Filtering, Rate Limiting, and Headers

content: Visualizing Defense in Depthgraph LRAttacker[Attacker] -->|Request| FW[Firewall/WAF]FW -->|Allowed| IP[1. IP Filter Middleware]IP -->|Blocked IP| 403[403 Forbidden]IP -->|Allowed IP| Rate[2. Rate Limiter]Rate -->|Too Fast| 429[429 Too Many Requests]Rate -->|OK| Auth[3. Auth Middleware]Auth -->|Invalid Token| 401[401 Unauthorized]Auth -->|Valid User| Logic[Business Logic]Logic -->|Response| Headers[4. Secure Headers]Headers -->|Safe HTML| Client[User Browser]
title: Fortifying the Backend: Advanced IP Filtering, Rate Limiting, and Headers

content: 1. Custom IP Filtering MiddlewareWhile firewalls (AWS WAF, Cloudflare) are your first line of defense, adding application-level filtering gives you granular control. You can dynamically block IPs based on application behavior (e.g., “5 failed logins in 1 minute”).
title: Fortifying the Backend: Advanced IP Filtering, Rate Limiting, and Headers

content: 1.1 The Challenge: “Real” IP AddressIn a containerized environment (Docker/Kubernetes) or behind a Reverse Proxy (Nginx), RemoteAddr gets obscured. It usually shows the IP of the internal docker gateway (e.g., 172.18.0.1). The Solution: We must trust distinct headers, but only from trusted proxies. // internal/ipFilter/ip_filter.go source analysis func GetRealIP(req *http.Request) string { // 1. Check X-Forwarded-For (Standard) // Format: client, proxy1, proxy2 xff := req.Header.Get("X-Forwarded-For") if xff != "" { parts := strings.Split(xff, ",") return strings.TrimSpace(parts[0]) // First IP is the client } // 2. Check X-Real-IP (Nginx specific) xri := req.Header.Get("X-Real-IP") if xri != "" { return xri } // 3. Fallback to RemoteAddr (strip port) ip, _, _ := net.SplitHostPort(req.RemoteAddr) return ip }
title: Fortifying the Backend: Advanced IP Filtering, Rate Limiting, and Headers

content: 1.2 Implementing the BlocklistWe maintain a list of banned CIDRs (Classless Inter-Domain Routing). This allows us to block single IPs (192.168.1.5/32) or entire subnets (10.0.0.0/8). type IPFilter struct { bannedSubnets []*net.IPNet } func NewIPFilter(bannedList []string) *IPFilter { var subnets []*net.IPNet for _, cidr := range bannedList { _, network, err := net.ParseCIDR(cidr) if err != nil { // Handle error: maybe log specific bad entry continue } subnets = append(subnets, network) } return &IPFilter{bannedSubnets: subnets} } func (f *IPFilter) IsBanned(ipStr string) bool { parsedIP := net.ParseIP(ipStr) if parsedIP == nil { return false // Malformed IP, technically safely ignored or strictly blocked } for _, subnet := range f.bannedSubnets { if subnet.Contains(parsedIP) { return true } } return false } Middleware Integration: func (f *IPFilter) Middleware(next echo.HandlerFunc) echo.HandlerFunc { return func(c echo.Context) error { ip := GetRealIP(c.Request()) if f.IsBanned(ip) { // Return 403 Forbidden // Optionally: Log this attempt to a security audit log return echo.NewHTTPError(http.StatusForbidden, "Access Denied by IP Policy") } return next(c) } }
title: Fortifying the Backend: Advanced IP Filtering, Rate Limiting, and Headers

content: 2. Rate Limiting (Traffic Control)Rate limiting protects your resources from exhaustion (CPU/Memory/DB Connections) and prevents brute-force attacks.
title: Fortifying the Backend: Advanced IP Filtering, Rate Limiting, and Headers

content: 2.1 Token Bucket Algorithm (Conceptual)Imagine a bucket that holds Tokens. The bucket has a maximum capacity (e.g., 5 tokens). New tokens “drip” into the bucket at a constant rate (e.g., 1 token per second). When a request comes in, it must take a token to proceed. If the bucket is empty, the request is rejected (429 Too Many Requests). This allows for Bursty traffic (the user can make 5 fast requests) but enforces a long-term Average rate.
title: Fortifying the Backend: Advanced IP Filtering, Rate Limiting, and Headers

content: 2.2 Implementation in EchoWe use echo-middleware/rate (or similar libraries like golang.org/x/time/rate). import ( "golang.org/x/time/rate" "github.com/labstack/echo/v4/middleware" ) func RateLimitConfig() middleware.RateLimiterConfig { return middleware.RateLimiterConfig{ Skipper: middleware.DefaultSkipper, Store: middleware.NewRateLimiterMemoryStoreWithConfig( middleware.RateLimiterMemoryStoreConfig{Rate: rate.Limit(10), Burst: 30, ExpiresIn: 3 * time.Minute}, ), IdentifierExtractor: func(ctx echo.Context) (string, error) { // Rate limit based on IP address return ctx.RealIP(), nil, }, ErrorHandler: func(context echo.Context, err error) error { return context.JSON(http.StatusTooManyRequests, map[string]string{ "error": "Rate limit exceeded. Please slow down.", }) }, DenyHandler: func(context echo.Context, identifier string, err error) error { return context.JSON(http.StatusTooManyRequests, map[string]string{ "error": "Rate limit exceeded", }) }, } } Advanced Strategy: We don’t just apply one global limit. We apply different limits to different routes: Public API (GET /posts): High limit (e.g., 100 req/min). Auth API (POST /login): Strict limit (e.g., 5 req/min) to prevent credential stuffing.
title: Fortifying the Backend: Advanced IP Filtering, Rate Limiting, and Headers

content: 3. Secure HTTP HeadersHeaders are instructions to the browser on how to behave securely.
title: Fortifying the Backend: Advanced IP Filtering, Rate Limiting, and Headers

content: 3.1 Key Headers Explained Header Value Purpose X-Content-Type-Options nosniff Tells the browser not to guess the file type. If we send a file as text/plain, Chrome shouldn’t try to execute it as JavaScript even if it looks like code. X-Frame-Options DENY or SAMEORIGIN Prevents Clickjacking. It ensures your site cannot be embedded in an <iframe> on an attacker’s site (where they might overlay invisible buttons). X-XSS-Protection 1; mode=block (Legacy) Activates browser’s built-in XSS filter. Strict-Transport-Security max-age=31536000 HSTS. Tells the browser “Only talk to me over HTTPS”. Even if the user types http://, the browser upgrades the request internally. Content-Security-Policy default-src 'self' CSP. The holy grail. It defines exactly where scripts, images, and styles can load from.
title: Fortifying the Backend: Advanced IP Filtering, Rate Limiting, and Headers

content: 3.2 Implementation in GoCalls to c.Response().Header().Set(k, v) in a middleware ensure these are present on every response, even 404s. func SecureHeadersMiddleware(next echo.HandlerFunc) echo.HandlerFunc { return func(c echo.Context) error { header := c.Response().Header() header.Set("X-Frame-Options", "DENY") header.Set("X-Content-Type-Options", "nosniff") header.Set("X-XSS-Protection", "1; mode=block") header.Set("Strict-Transport-Security", "max-age=31536000; includeSubDomains") // A rigid CSP example csp := "default-src 'self'; script-src 'self' 'unsafe-inline' https://trusted.cdn.com; img-src 'self' data: https:;" header.Set("Content-Security-Policy", csp) return next(c) } }
title: Fortifying the Backend: Advanced IP Filtering, Rate Limiting, and Headers

content: 3.3 Sanitize Request ModelsWe must also scrub input. We use basic strippers on JSON input. import "strings" func SanitizeInput(input string) string { // Basic example: Remove html tags // In production, use "github.com/microcosm-cc/bluemonday" return strings.ReplaceAll(input, "<script>", "") }
title: Fortifying the Backend: Advanced IP Filtering, Rate Limiting, and Headers

content: 4. Data Leakage PreventionOne common security flaw is Data Leakage in API Responses. Example: Returning the entire User struct in a JSON response. // BAD type User struct { ID string `json:"id"` Password string `json:"password"` // OOPS! This gets sent to the client! } The Fix: Use DTOs (Data Transfer Objects) or explicit JSON tags. // GOOD type User struct { ID string `json:"id"` Password string `json:"-"` // Dash always ignores this field } // BETTER: Explicit Response Struct type UserResponse struct { ID string `json:"id"` Email string `json:"email"` Role string `json:"role"` } func ToUserResponse(u *User) UserResponse { return UserResponse{ ID: u.ID, Email: u.Email, Role: u.Role, } } At Golang4U, we adhere to strict DTO usage. The Service layer returns domain models, and the Handler layer converts them to DTOs before sending. This acts as a firewall for your data structure.
title: Fortifying the Backend: Advanced IP Filtering, Rate Limiting, and Headers

content: ConclusionSecurity is not a feature; it’s a mindset. By implementing: IP Filtering to reduce the attack surface, Rate Limiting to mitigate abuse, Secure Headers to protect the client, and DTOs to prevent leaks, We create a robust backend that is resilient against the most common web attacks. In the next post, we discuss Authentication and why we chose PASETO over the industry-standard JWT.
title: Fortifying the Backend: Advanced IP Filtering, Rate Limiting, and Headers

content: A comprehensive, 20-minute read on the Clean Architecture of Golang4U. We cover the rationale behind Echo & MongoDB, dependency injection, and the lifecycle of a request from ingress to database.
title: Building a Production-Grade Go Backend: The Golang4U Architecture Deep Dive

content: IntroductionIn the world of Go application development, “structure” is a topic of endless debate. Should you use a flat structure? Group by feature? Follow “Standard Go Project Layout”? With Golang4U, we aimed to build a system that is robust enough for enterprise use cases but simple enough to be maintained by a small team. We adopted a Service-Oriented layered architecture (often called Clean Architecture or Hexagonal Architecture lite) to ensure separation of concerns, testability, and scalability. In this deep dive, we will explore: The Tech Stack Decisions: Why Echo? Why MongoDB? The Project Structure: Mapping the internal folder. Dependency Injection: How we wire it all together without global state. Request Lifecycle: Tracing a request from the user’s browser to the database and back.
title: Building a Production-Grade Go Backend: The Golang4U Architecture Deep Dive

content: 1. The Tech Stack decisionsEvery architectural choice comes with trade-offs. Here is why we chose our specific stack.
title: Building a Production-Grade Go Backend: The Golang4U Architecture Deep Dive

content: 1.1 The Web Framework: Echo (v4)Go’s standard net/http library is powerful, but for a production REST API, you often find yourself rewriting the same boilerplate: routing with parameters, group middleware, data binding, and response formatting. We chose Echo for three main reasons: Performance: Echo’s router is highly optimized, with zero dynamic memory allocation for route dispatching. Middleware Ecosystem: It has a robust suite of built-in middleware (Recover, Logger, CORS, Secure) that are production-ready out of the box. Context Interface: The echo.Context interface simplifies request handling significantly. Code Example: The Power of Binding In standard Go, parsing a JSON body involves creating a decoder and handling EOF errors manually. In Echo: type LoginRequest struct { Email string `json:"email" validate:"required,email"` Password string `json:"password" validate:"required"` } func (h *AuthHandler) Login(c echo.Context) error { var req LoginRequest // Bind() handles JSON, XML, Form data automatically based on Content-Type if err := c.Bind(&req); err != nil { return c.JSON(http.StatusBadRequest, map[string]string{"error": "Invalid request format"}) } // ... validation and logic ... }
title: Building a Production-Grade Go Backend: The Golang4U Architecture Deep Dive

content: 1.2 The Database: MongoDBWe chose MongoDB (NoSQL) over a traditional relational database (PostgreSQL/MySQL) for specific reasons related to our domain: Content Management: Blog posts, comments, and tags are inherently hierarchical and document-oriented. A post has embedded comments, arrays of tags, and dynamic metadata. Storing this in a single document avoids complex JOIN operations. Schema Flexibility: As we iterate on User Profiles (adding social links, preferences, 2FA secrets), we can update the struct in Go without running heavy migration scripts on the database. Read Performance: For a read-heavy application (viewing feeds), fetching a single document is generally faster than joining 4-5 tables. Go Driver: We use the official go.mongodb.org/mongo-driver/v2.
title: Building a Production-Grade Go Backend: The Golang4U Architecture Deep Dive

content: 2. The Project StructureWe follow the Standard Go Project Layout, designed to separate public API code from internal business logic. This isn’t just arbitrary; it prevents “import cycles” and forces you to think about dependencies.
title: Building a Production-Grade Go Backend: The Golang4U Architecture Deep Dive

content: 2.1 The “Clean Architecture” Mapgraph TDsubgraph "External World"Client[User Browser/Mobile]DB[(MongoDB)]endsubgraph "Interface Layer (Transport)"Handler[HTTP Handlers (Echo)]endsubgraph "Core Business Logic"Service[Service Layer]endsubgraph "Data Access"Repo[Repository Layer]endClient -->|HTTP Request| HandlerHandler -->|DTO| ServiceService -->|Domain Model| RepoRepo -->|BSON| DB
title: Building a Production-Grade Go Backend: The Golang4U Architecture Deep Dive

content: 2.2 The Directory Treegraph LRRoot[Project Root]Root --> Cmd[cmd/]Root --> Internal[internal/]Cmd --> Main[main.go (Wiring)]Internal --> Handler[handler/ (HTTP)]Internal --> Service[service/ (Logic)]Internal --> Repo[repository/ (DB)]Internal --> Model[model/ (Structs)]Internal --> Middleware[middleware/ (Security)]
title: Building a Production-Grade Go Backend: The Golang4U Architecture Deep Dive

content: 2.3 cmd/server/main.go: The Composition RootThe main package is the only place where all layers meet. It performs Dependency Injection. Config: Loads config.toml. Infra: Connects to Mongo/Redis. Wiring: Injects Repo into Service, and Service into Handler. Run: Starts the HTTP listener.
title: Building a Production-Grade Go Backend: The Golang4U Architecture Deep Dive

content: 2.4 internal/model: The Shared LanguageThis package contains Pure Data Structures. It has zero dependencies on other internal packages. // internal/model/user.go type User struct { ID string `bson:"_id,omitempty" json:"id"` Email string `bson:"email" json:"email"` Profile Profile `bson:"profile" json:"profile"` // Password is NOT in JSON for security Password string `bson:"password" json:"-"` }
title: Building a Production-Grade Go Backend: The Golang4U Architecture Deep Dive

content: 2.3 internal/repository (Data Access Layer)Responsibility: Talk to the database. This layer knows how to store things (BSON, SQL queries) but doesn’t know why. It performs CRUD operations. Idiom: We accept interfaces or specific structs and return domain models. // internal/repository/user_repository.go type UserRepository struct { collection *mongo.Collection } func NewUserRepository(db *mongo.Database) *UserRepository { return &UserRepository{ collection: db.Collection("users"), } } func (r *UserRepository) FindByEmail(ctx context.Context, email string) (*model.User, error) { var user model.User // Use a context with timeout for production safety ctx, cancel := context.WithTimeout(ctx, 5*time.Second) defer cancel() err := r.collection.FindOne(ctx, bson.M{"email": email}).Decode(&user) if err != nil { if errors.Is(err, mongo.ErrNoDocuments) { return nil, nil // Not found is not always an error } return nil, err } return &user, nil }
title: Building a Production-Grade Go Backend: The Golang4U Architecture Deep Dive

content: 2.4 internal/service (Business Logic Layer)Responsibility: The brain of the application. It validates business rules, combines data from multiple repositories, and handles external APIs (email, payment). Example Rule: “A user cannot register with an email that is already blocked.” // internal/service/auth_service.go type AuthService struct { userRepo *repository.UserRepository ipFilter *ipfilter.Service } func (s *AuthService) RegisterUser(req model.RegisterRequest) error { // 1. Check if email exists existing, _ := s.userRepo.FindByEmail(context.Background(), req.Email) if existing != nil { return errors.New("email already taken") } // 2. Hash Password (bcrypt/argon2) hashed, _ := bcrypt.GenerateFromPassword([]byte(req.Password), 14) // 3. Create User Model newUser := model.User{ Email: req.Email, Password: string(hashed), } // 4. Save return s.userRepo.Create(context.Background(), &newUser) }
title: Building a Production-Grade Go Backend: The Golang4U Architecture Deep Dive

content: 2.5 internal/handler (Transport Layer)Responsibility: Speak HTTP. It reads the echo.Context, parses requests, calls the Service, and formats the Response. Crucial Rule: The handler should rarely have if statements related to business logic. It should just handle input parsing and output formatting.
title: Building a Production-Grade Go Backend: The Golang4U Architecture Deep Dive

content: 3. Dependency Injection (WIring)Go doesn’t have a “Magic Container” like Spring Boot (Java) or NestJS, and that’s a good thing. We favor Explicit Dependency Injection. We manually pass dependencies into constructors (New... functions). This happens in main.go. It makes the dependency graph obvious and makes testing easy (we can pass mocks implementation). // Main wiring in main.go func main() { // 1. Infrastructure mongoClient := connectMongo() db := mongoClient.Database("golang4u") // 2. Repositories userRepo := repository.NewUserRepository(db) postRepo := repository.NewPostRepository(db) // 3. Services (injected with Repositories) authService := service.NewAuthService(userRepo) postService := service.NewPostService(postRepo) // 4. Handlers (injected with Services) authHandler := handler.NewAuthHandler(authService) postHandler := handler.NewPostHandler(postService) // 5. Routes e := echo.New() e.POST("/login", authHandler.Login) }
title: Building a Production-Grade Go Backend: The Golang4U Architecture Deep Dive

content: 4. Request Lifecycle: A Step-by-Step FlowLet’s visualize what happens when a user clicks “Log In”. sequenceDiagramparticipant Clientparticipant Middlewareparticipant Handlerparticipant Serviceparticipant Repositoryparticipant DatabaseClient->>Middleware: POST /login (JSON)Middleware->>Middleware: Logger & Rate Limit checkMiddleware->>Handler: Pass RequestHandler->>Handler: Bind JSON to StructHandler->>Handler: Validate (Required fields)Handler->>Service: Login(email, password)Service->>Repository: FindByEmail(email)Repository->>Database: db.users.findOne({email: ...})Database-->>Repository: User DocumentRepository-->>Service: User ModelService->>Service: CompareHash(password, user.Hash)Service-->>Handler: Return User/ErrorHandler->>Handler: Generate PASETO TokenHandler-->>Client: 200 OK {token: "..."}
title: Building a Production-Grade Go Backend: The Golang4U Architecture Deep Dive

content: Detailed Breakdown Ingress: The request hits the server. Middleware Chain: Recovery: Ensures if the handlers panic, the server doesn’t crash. CORS: Checks if the request is coming from an allowed origin (golang4u.com). IPFilter: Checks if the IP is in our Redis blocklist. Logger: Logs path=/login status=... latency=... for observability. Handler: func (h *AuthHandler) Login is called. It parses the JSON body. Service: authService.Login performs the password comparison. It avoids returning specific errors like “User not found” to prevent user enumeration attacks; instead, it returns “Invalid Credentials”. Response: The handler wraps the result in a standard JSON envelope: {"data": ..., "status": "success"}.
title: Building a Production-Grade Go Backend: The Golang4U Architecture Deep Dive

content: 5. Advanced Topcs
title: Building a Production-Grade Go Backend: The Golang4U Architecture Deep Dive

content: 5.1 Context UsageIn Go, context.Context is the lifeline of a request. It carries concepts of: Deadlines: “Stop this DB query if it takes > 2 seconds”. Cancellation: “The user closed the browser, stop processing”. We pass ctx from Handler -> Service -> Repository. MongoDB respects this context. // Creating a child context with timeout ctx, cancel := context.WithTimeout(c.Request().Context(), 2*time.Second) defer cancel() user, err := h.service.GetUser(ctx, id)
title: Building a Production-Grade Go Backend: The Golang4U Architecture Deep Dive

content: 5.2 Error Handling vs LoggingWe don’t log errors in the Repository. We return them. We don’t log errors in the Service. We return them. We log errors in the Handler. Why? If you log everywhere, your logs become spam. “Failed to query DB” would appear 3 times (Repo log, Service log, Handler log). By bubbling the error up, the Handler decides: 500 Internal Error: Log the full stack trace for devs. Return “Something went wrong” to user. 400 Bad Request: Don’t log (user error). Return proper message to user.
title: Building a Production-Grade Go Backend: The Golang4U Architecture Deep Dive

content: ConclusionThe architectural choices in Golang4U provide a stable foundation. By strictly separating Transport (HTTP) from Logic from Storage, we create a codebase that is easy to navigate and safe to modify. Dependencies flow inwards, and data flows downwards. In the next post of this series, we will look at how we secure this architecture using Advanced Security Middleware like Custom IP Filtering and Token Buckets.
title: Building a Production-Grade Go Backend: The Golang4U Architecture Deep Dive
